concept.shortExplanation: One attention pattern per layer would force every relationship a sentence contains through a single set of weights. Instead the layer splits its dimensions into several heads, each with its own query, key and value projections, each computing an independent pattern, and concatenates the results. Nothing assigns roles to heads — but train the model and heads reliably specialise anyway, some tracking position, some syntax, some parking on delimiters. You are about to extract all of them from a real model and measure what each one does.
concept.ahaMoment: Head specialisation was never designed. It is what happens when you give a model several parallel channels and a loss that rewards using them for different things.

levels.title: Spot the Specialist
levels.instructions: All twelve heads of this layer, side by side, computed live. Find the head that attends almost entirely to the previous token — its behaviour is measured directly from its real attention matrix.

engineConfig.sentence: the quiet librarian returned the overdue book yesterday morning

hints: Look at layer 0 first. Earlier layers are where raw positional patterns like "attend to the previous token" tend to show up most cleanly, before later layers drift toward delimiter-heavy attention.
A previous-token head's matrix has weight concentrated one cell to the left of the diagonal in almost every row. Scan the twelve mini-matrices for that stripe rather than reading the numbers.

At layer 0, head 2 attends to the immediately preceding token with about 0.83 average weight, and it's the only head at that layer classified previous-token — every other head is diffuse. Nominate head 2 in all three rounds for a perfect score.

solution.problem: Twelve attention heads run in parallel at every layer, and they do not all do the same thing. Each head's behaviour here is measured from its own real attention matrix — how much weight it puts on the previous token, the next one, itself, punctuation, or nothing in particular. You nominate a head that specialises in attending to the previous token, three times.

steps.title: Know what the labels mean mechanically
steps.body: A previous-token head puts most of each row's weight one position back. A delimiter head parks its weight on punctuation or sentence boundaries. A self head attends mostly to the token itself. Diffuse means no strong pattern — the row is spread out. These are measurements of the matrix, not interpretations of it.

steps.title: Look at layer 0 first
steps.body: Early layers are where the mechanical, position-based heads live, because there is not yet much semantic content to attend to. Later layers are where the content-driven behaviour from chapter 5.2 appears. Starting at layer 0 is the fastest route to a clean specialist.

steps.title: Find the one head that is doing it
steps.body: At layer 0 of this model, head 2 attends to the immediately preceding token with about 0.83 average weight — and it is the only head at that layer classified as previous-token. Every other head there measures as diffuse. Specialisation is real but sparse: one head in twelve.

steps.title: Use the same head every round
steps.body: All three rounds ask for the same behaviour, and there is only one head at this layer that has it, so nominating head 2 three times is a perfect score. That is not a loophole — it is the finding.

solution.answer: Nominate head 2 in all three rounds — the only previous-token specialist at layer 0, at about 0.83 average weight. Autofill nominates whichever head the level's own measurement identifies.
solution.takeaway: Multi-head attention is not twelve copies of the same computation. Heads differentiate during training into recognisable roles, and the fact that you can point at one and say what it does is the foundation of mechanistic interpretability.

levels.title: Classify Every Head
levels.instructions: Assign a behaviour label to each head in the layer. Ground truth comes from statistics computed over each head's real attention matrix — offset concentration, entropy and delimiter mass.

engineConfig.sentence: after the meeting ended, the team walked to the cafe across the street

hints: Not every head has a clean label. Heads whose top two behaviour scores are close together are excluded from grading entirely — this level's margin is 0.12, so spend your effort on the heads with an unambiguous pattern rather than guessing on borderline ones.
A delimiter head lights up a whole column at [CLS] or [SEP] no matter which row (query) you look at. A diffuse head has no strong single pattern — weight spread out fairly evenly across the row.

At layer 2, 7 of the 12 heads are gradable: heads 0, 4, 7, 9 and 11 are delimiter specialists; heads 6 and 10 are diffuse. Heads 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 fall below the confidence margin and aren't graded either way. Labelling those 7 correctly scores a perfect 1.0.

solution.problem: All twelve heads of layer 2 at once, and a label for each. Only heads whose measurement is clear-cut are graded — a head sitting between two behaviours has no defensible answer — so the score is over the gradable subset rather than all twelve.

steps.title: Check which heads are even in play
steps.body: At layer 2, 7 of the 12 heads clear the confidence margin. Heads 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 fall below it and are not graded either way, so a wrong label on those costs nothing and a right one earns nothing. Five of twelve heads doing something genuinely ambiguous is itself worth noticing.

steps.title: Label the delimiter cluster
steps.body: Heads 0, 4, 7, 9 and 11 are all delimiter specialists — they park their attention on punctuation and boundary tokens. Five heads in one layer doing the same job looks redundant, and it partly is: heads are not independently useful, and pruning studies routinely remove a third of them with little loss.

steps.title: Label the diffuse pair
steps.body: Heads 6 and 10 measure as diffuse: no position or token type dominates their rows. Diffuse is a real classification here, not a failure to classify — a head spreading attention broadly is doing averaging work, which is useful even though it is not interpretable as a rule.

steps.title: Read what the layer is doing overall
steps.body: Layer 2 has no previous-token, next-token or self specialists at all. The mechanical position heads were at layer 0; by layer 2 the model has moved on to structure. Watching that shift across layers is the point of the layer slider.

solution.answer: Heads 0, 4, 7, 9 and 11 → delimiter; heads 6 and 10 → diffuse. The other five are below the confidence margin and are not graded. Labelling those seven correctly is a perfect 1.0 and three stars. Autofill labels every head with its measured behaviour.
solution.takeaway: Interpretability is a measurement discipline with a lot of ambiguity in it. Five of twelve heads here have no clean label, and reporting that honestly — rather than forcing every head into a category — is what makes the other seven trustworthy.

levels.title: Which Head Solves It?
levels.instructions: Your own sentence, containing a long-range dependency. Find the single head anywhere in the model that most strongly links the two tokens you care about, and see how localised that capability really is.

engineConfig.sentence: the keys that the neighbour returned last week are still on the table

hints: The default sentence hides a subject-verb pair split by a relative clause: "the keys that the neighbour returned last week are still on the table." The verb "are" has to agree with "keys", many tokens earlier — that split is the long-range dependency to hunt for.

Attention isn't symmetric — the direction you probe matters, and the answer isn't always in the layer you start on. Probe from the later token back to the earlier one, and move the layer slider since the search spans every layer, not just the one shown.
Probing from "are" (token 9) back to "keys" (token 2) at layer 3, head 1 finds a weight of 0.896 — the strongest link for that pair anywhere in the model, so it scores a perfect 1.0.

solution.problem: 'The keys that the neighbour returned last week are still on the table.' The verb 'are' agrees with 'keys', not with 'week' or 'neighbour', across an entire relative clause. You pick the token pair and then hunt for the head anywhere in the model that carries that link most strongly; the score is your best find divided by the strongest link that actually exists.

steps.title: Choose the pair that matters
steps.body: The interesting dependency is from 'are' (token 9) back to 'keys' (token 2) — seven tokens apart, with two other plural-looking nouns in between. If the model gets subject-verb agreement right here, something has to be carrying that link.

steps.title: Search across layers, not just within one
steps.body: This level searches every layer, and that matters: the strongest link for this pair is not at the layer the board opens on. A head that does nothing interesting for most pairs can be the one that carries this one.

steps.title: Find the head
steps.body: Layer 3, head 1 gives a weight of 0.896 between 'are' and 'keys' — the strongest link for that pair anywhere in this model, and a very high weight for a single attention entry. That is a specific head, in a specific layer, doing a specific grammatical job.

steps.title: Understand the scoring
steps.body: The score divides what you found by the best that exists for your chosen pair, so it rewards searching thoroughly rather than hitting a number. It also means a badly chosen pair is still winnable — the level asks you to find the best head for the dependency you named, whatever you named.

solution.answer: Probe from 'are' (token 9) back to 'keys' (token 2), and take layer 3, head 1 — weight 0.896, the strongest link for that pair in the model, for a perfect 1.0 and three stars. Autofill sets that pair if you have not chosen one and probes the strongest head it can find.
solution.takeaway: Long-range grammatical agreement is carried by identifiable heads, which is the clearest demonstration in this course that attention is doing something structured rather than statistical smearing. It is also why head-level analysis is a real research method rather than a visualisation gimmick.
